opus-5.5.text:
I think the emphasis makes a lot of sense, and it's a bet I broadly share. When people say "robotics brain," they usually mean a general-purpose model that can take in vision and language and output actions, and that can transfer across tasks and maybe across different robot bodies. Physical Intelligence is clearly betting that this is the bottleneck. Hardware has gotten good enough and cheap enough that what's missing is the intelligence to make it useful in unstructured environments.

That said, I'd add a few nuances.

First, the brain and the body aren't fully separable. A lot of what looks like "intelligence" in manipulation is really co-designed with the hardware: the hand, the compliance, the sensing, the control loop. If you treat the brain as a pure software layer sitting on top of arbitrary hardware, you can run into limits. The physical interface matters, especially for contact-rich tasks.

Second, data is really the core question, more than model architecture. In language models we had the internet. In robotics we don't have an equivalent corpus of action data. So the question becomes: how do you collect it at scale? Teleoperation, simulation, human video, deployment in the field? Each has tradeoffs in cost, diversity, and how well it transfers. I think the companies that win will be the ones that figure out a scalable data flywheel, not just the ones with the best model.

Third, there's a question of timing and evaluation. It's easy to make impressive demos. It's much harder to get the kind of reliability, 99.9% and beyond, that real deployment needs. Generalization in robotics is still pretty brittle. So I'm optimistic about the direction, but I think we should be honest that we're early, maybe somewhere around where language models were before scaling really clicked.

So overall, I think focusing on the brain is the right long-term bet. But the people who'll make it work will also deeply understand hardware, data collection, and the messy details of the physical world. It can't just be a pure AI play transplanted from language.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what Pi and Scale are both doing right now is actually quite telling about where the whole field believes the bottleneck is. For a long time, people assumed robotics was a hardware problem. If you just built a better arm, a more dexterous hand, cheaper actuators, the intelligence would follow. What we've learned over the past two or three years is almost the opposite. The hardware is good enough, maybe not perfect, but good enough. What's missing is the brain, the thing that can look at a messy kitchen it has never seen before and figure out what to do.

So when Pi talks about a general-purpose robot foundation model, they're essentially making a bet that the same recipe that worked for language, scale plus diversity plus a flexible architecture, will work for physical action. And I think they're partially right. The early results, where one policy transfers across very different robot bodies, are genuinely impressive. That was not obvious even a few years ago.

Scale's angle is a bit different, and I find it interesting because it's a data company's view of the problem. Their argument is that the brain is only as good as what you feed it, and physical world data is incredibly expensive and fragmented compared to text. So they're positioning themselves as the pipeline, the layer that collects, cleans, and labels embodied data at a volume nobody else can. In a sense they're saying, you worry about the model, we'll worry about making sure it has enough to learn from.

Where I'd push back a little on both of them is this. Language models had the internet. Robotics does not have an internet of actions. Teleoperation data is slow, simulation has a reality gap, and video of humans is useful but not the same as robot experience. So the question I keep coming back to is whether the brain-first emphasis is premature, or whether it's exactly what forces the data problem to finally get solved. My honest view is that the brain and the body can't really be separated the way the current narrative suggests. The companies that win are going to be the ones that treat them as one system, and iterate on both at the same time.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a bet on where the bottleneck in robotics is moving. You can build a capable physical machine, but getting it to handle unfamiliar situations reliably is still difficult. The robotics brain is about turning perception and instructions into useful action, and ideally doing that across tasks rather than training a separate system for each one.

That makes the emphasis understandable. But I’d be careful about equating a better model with a complete robotics solution. The brain, the body, and the data collection process have to work together. A compelling demonstration is one thing; recovering from mistakes and operating reliably over long periods is another.

So the question I’d ask of both Pi and Scale is: does their approach create a learning loop where deployment produces useful experience, and that experience makes the next deployment better? That would matter more to me than who has the most impressive demo.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the emphasis makes sense. The brain is where you try to turn perception into useful action: understanding the environment, deciding what to do, and adapting when something changes. But I’d separate an impressive demonstration from a system that works reliably. A robot has to deal with the consequences of its actions in the physical world.

For Pi and Scale, the question I’d focus on is how they build that learning loop. Can they collect useful experience, identify failures, and turn those failures into better behavior across different tasks? The model matters, but so do the data and the evaluation. I’m interested in whether progress transfers beyond the settings the robot has already seen.
